source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Soar raises an impasse when the decision procedure cannot pick or apply an operator. Three types are named in the text: state no-change, operator tie/conflict, operator no-change. The glossary lists four (conflict split from tie).
numbers: 3 impasse types in Section 3 text; 4 in the glossary
quote: State no-change: No operators are proposed.
limits: Operator no-change can also just mean a slow external action; the right response is then to wait, not to subgoal.
agent_relevance: S6 trigger design: copy the typed triggers (nothing to try, several options and no way to choose, chosen option makes no progress). The third type needs a check for slow actions so we do not treat a long tool call as a failure.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: A substate is a new state linked to the superstate. Reasoning in it uses the same decision cycle, so it is meta-level work: propose, evaluate and apply operators about the stuck decision. Substates can nest into a stack. An impasse ends when a new decision can be made or a different impasse appears.
numbers: one substate per state; stack depth not capped in the text
limits: Cost: deliberate substate work is slower than rule firing.
agent_relevance: Subgoal in S6 should re-enter the same loop (S1) with a state line naming the parent, not a separate mode. Matches the schema design.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Chunking runs whenever a result is created in a substate. It back-traces the rules that made the result. Superstate elements that were tested become conditions; the result becomes the action. Independent results give several rules. Only what was actually referenced enters the rule, which is the source of generality.
numbers: no numbers; mechanism description
quote: Chunking is automatic and is invoked whenever a result is created in a substate.
limits: Requires deterministic substate decisions; not used when decisions rest on numeric preferences.
agent_relevance: Library entry should store only the conditions the subgoal really used, not the whole context. That keeps the stored subgoal general and cheap to match.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Chunks learned per impasse type: tie/conflict gives evaluation (search-control) rules, state no-change gives operator-proposal rules, operator no-change gives operator-application rules, plus elaborations. Planning in a substate becomes search control.
numbers: 4 rule kinds
limits: Early demos of some kinds were thin (see a10).
agent_relevance: Library should record the impasse type with each entry, since a tie fix (a preference) is a different object from a no-change fix (a method).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Reimplemented chunking (EBBS, Assanie 2022) aims at rules that are correct and as general as possible. The author reports the analysis overhead is minimal and the gains much larger than the costs.
numbers: claim attributed to Assanie (2022); no figures in this paper
limits: Cost claim is secondhand here; see a16 for the manual's example.
agent_relevance: Cost of building library entries is likely small next to LLM calls, but verify in our own logs.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: As experience accumulates, processing levels move down: substate work becomes rules. The author maps this loosely to System 2 becoming System 1, with the caution that Kahneman's System 1 also contains more than rules.
numbers: qualitative
limits: Mapping is suggestive, not tested.
agent_relevance: Frames the library as a way for repeated slow reasoning to become fast lookups, which is the point of S9 memory.

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by chunking: summary of a task and a model
finding: Chunking theory of learning: chunks are stored patterns built from existing chunks. Three assumptions: performance (a chunk is processed faster than its parts, given a serial bottleneck plus a parallel part), learning (chunks learned at a constant average rate), task structure (larger patterns recur less often). Together they predict the power law of practice T = B*N^-a.
numbers: Seibel (1963) 1023-choice task, ten lights and ten buttons; human power-law data over more than 75,000 trials (76,725 plotted); model run by hand on 9 trials (left hand, 5 lights)
quote: performance can be improved by acquiring higher-level chunks
limits: This is Xaps2, a pre-Soar production system; no goals or impasses yet. Model is one short run plus a meta-model.
agent_relevance: Origin of compile slow work into fast lookup. The bottleneck assumption warns that chunks help only where there is a serial cost to cut; for an LLM agent that cost is calls and tokens.

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by chunking: summary of a task and a model
finding: Simulation of the chunking model on the Seibel task. A meta-model estimated production cycles as 13 per trial plus 31 per pattern used. A chunk was learned with fixed probability 0.01 when possible, because learning at every chance finished the task in about log2(10), between 3 and 4, passes.
numbers: simulated 72,633 trials; 1023 trials per pass; curve straight on log-log axes
limits: The 0.01 learning probability is a free parameter added to match the data. The fitted constants were garbled in the PDF text and are not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Warns that a learning rate is a tuned knob. In a library, an admission threshold will be a similar knob.

source: Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed: the case for an exponential law of practice
finding: Challenge to the power law that chunking theory was built to explain. In unaveraged data the exponential fit better than the power function in all data sets; averaging across learners or conditions biases toward the power law.
numbers: 40 data sets, 7,910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments. Seibel subject J.K. averaged data: power R2 .9858, exponential .9584, APEX .9902 (general power .9895). Brown & Heathcote 4-key task: 76.4% of series better fit by exponential.
quote: The power function is treated as the law relating response time to practice trials. However, the evidence for a power law is flawed
limits: Does not refute chunking itself; a chunking account of exponential learning is discussed. Same-subject Seibel re-analysis by Rosenbloom & Newell (1987b) also favoured exponential.
agent_relevance: Do not assume library gains follow a smooth power curve. Measure gain per entry directly.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom & Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: the anatomy of a general learning mechanism
finding: Defines a general learning mechanism by task, knowledge and aspect generality. Chunking acquires rules from goal-based experience; the problem solver gives the opportunities, the relevance bias and the consumer, and the rule memory integrates the result. Claims strategy acquisition and operator implementation were shown; other subgoal types were not yet demonstrated.
numbers: Eight Puzzle macro-table replication of Korf (1985a)
quote: The problem solver provides many things: the opportunities to learn, direction as to what is relevant
limits: The authors state that conflict impasses had not yet been met and problem-space selection was not yet problematic. The biggest coverage limit was problem-space creation and change of representation.
agent_relevance: Learning is tied to a working solver: store only what a subgoal produced, and expect no gain for changes of representation.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom & Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: the anatomy of a general learning mechanism
finding: Generality comes mainly from implicit generalization: only the working-memory elements referenced during problem solving become conditions. Only a small percentage of augmentations ended up in the example chunk. The object representation bounds how general chunks can be. If generality is lacking the mechanism is just a caching scheme.
numbers: Eight Puzzle chunks needed for Korf's macro table: 230 with no transfer (170 with search control), 112 simple transfer, 83 symmetry within column, 61 symmetry across column, 54 if non-minimal macros allowed (14% of problems +2 path length, 26% +4, 7% +6). Tower of Hanoi 3 disks: 8 chunks in one trial encode Korf's 6-macro table.
quote: If generality is lacking, and little transfer occurs, the learning mechanism is simply a caching scheme.
limits: Results depend on a hand-designed state representation that exposes topology. Counts for lower levels were computed by hand; the run was for the highest transfer level.
agent_relevance: Library entries will transfer only if the stored form drops irrelevant specifics. Chunk count per task is a useful measure of how well a library generalizes.

source: Tambe, Newell & Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks and its solution by restricting expressiveness
finding: Chunking cuts the number of actions a lot but can raise total time, because some learned rules are very costly to match. Cause is the match of single chunks, not their count. Three factors: multi-valued attributes and preferences, large condition footprints, bad condition ordering.
numbers: Cognitive effect (actions before/after): Eight-puzzle 6.53, 2-Queens 5.21, Grid 13.54, Magic-square 6.59, Syllogisms 11.59, Monkeys-Bananas 6.20, Waterjug 9.13, Farmer 11.09. Computational effect (time per action before/after): 0.15, 0.06, 0.06, 0.04, 0.89, 0.83, 0.57, 0.45. Magic-square total speedup 0.25 (four-fold slowdown); time per action up as much as 25x. Four of eight tasks slowed overall.
limits: Table columns were misaligned in extraction, so the pairing of values to tasks follows row order and per-task total speedups other than Magic-square are not recorded. Measured on Soar/PSM-E with a Rete matcher.
agent_relevance: Core warning for the library: fewer steps does not mean less cost. Retrieval and checking of stored subgoals must be bounded, or the library slows the agent.

source: Tambe, Newell & Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks and its solution by restricting expressiveness
finding: Fix: restrict the rule language (unique-attribute representation) so match cost grows only linearly with condition count. The price is that more chunks and more training problems are needed for the same generality. Smaller footprints also help.
numbers: Smaller footprint in Eight-puzzle: average condition elements 34 to 22, computational effect 0.15 to 0.25. Grid task: multi-attribute learned 17 chunks, tokens per action about 3 to 24, computational effect about 0.11 (about 9x slower); unique-attribute accumulated 142 (count as read) chunks to reach the same generality.
limits: Trade of cost bound versus expressiveness and generality; shown on small puzzle tasks.
agent_relevance: Prefer simple, flat stored entries with a cheap trigger test, even at the price of needing more entries.

source: Kim & Rosenbloom (1996) Learning efficient rules by maintaining the explanation structure
finding: Second source of slowdown: the match structure of the learned rule differs from the structure of the problem solving it came from. Making the learner keep that structure (non-linear rules) removes the slowdown. An earlier fix (Kim & Rosenbloom 1993) puts the search-control rules into the explanation so rules are not cut loose from the path actually taken.
numbers: Grid: average CPU 0.46 s without learning, 1.42 s linear-rule learning, 0.34 s non-linear-rule learning. Magic Square (9 sub-problems): linear learning ran out of memory (over 8 million tokens for one rule); non-linear was bounded by no-learning time and 9x faster than no learning.
limits: Two toy tasks; CPU seconds on one implementation. Also notes the average-growth effect: over one million rules can still be used efficiently (Doorenbos et al. 1992; Doorenbos 1993, not opened).
agent_relevance: Store the structure of the solution path with the entry, not only the conclusion, so a reused entry cannot cost more than redoing the work.

source: Rosenbloom & Aasman (1990) Knowledge level and inductive uses of chunking (EBL)
finding: Chunking is a form of explanation-based learning: new rules come from a dependency analysis of the traces of rules fired in subgoal problem solving. With a domain theory not all believed a priori, chunking can do rote learning and induction (version-space style), i.e. learn knowledge not implied by what is known. The non-penetrable memory assumption makes this more complicated.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; experiments not read in detail
limits: Only the framing parts of the paper were read this session.
agent_relevance: A solved subgoal can encode an unverified guess. Admit entries only after a test passes, since chunking by itself adds belief to whatever the substate concluded.

source: Soar Manual: Procedural Knowledge Learning
finding: Chunks are built when a subgoal creates a result in a superstate, at once, not at the end of the impasse. Learning is off by default. Learning modes include learning only at the bottom of the hierarchy. Bottom-up chunking: one result can yield several chunks as higher states match the first chunk.
numbers: EBBS example: arithmetic agent learned 1263 rules in Soar 9.4 but 8 rules in Soar 9.6
quote: In Soar 9.4, the arithmetic agent learns 1263 rules ... In Soar 9.6, the same agent only learns 8 rules
limits: Single example from the manual, no experiment described.
agent_relevance: Shows over-specific rules multiply fast (1263 vs 8). Library needs a generalize-and-merge step, or it fills with near-duplicates.

source: Soar Manual: Procedural Knowledge Learning
finding: Stale or wrong chunk handling: a chunk based on a particular search path can be over-specialized and simply will not match when the path differs; then the agent subgoals again and learns a similar chunk with different conditions. Justifications are temporary non-learned rules that can be over-general and are removed when their support ends.
numbers: qualitative
limits: Soar has no general mechanism to delete a bad chunk; correctness relies on EBBS analysis, which the manual says improves correctness and generality.
agent_relevance: Stale-entry rule: an entry that fails to match falls back to a fresh subgoal; an entry that matches and then fails should be demoted, which Soar does not give us for free.

source: Assanie (2022) Learning general and correct procedural knowledge in a cognitive architecture (PhD thesis, University of Michigan)
finding: Abstract level only (search snippet, thesis not opened). Defines correctness and generality for online procedural learning; four conditions for correct summarization; 12 correctness issues each remedied or detected by EBBS; evaluation on 14 agents across 8 domains.
numbers: 14 agents, 8 domains, 12 issues, 4 strategies (from abstract)
limits: Not opened; figures unverified.
agent_relevance: Candidate for angle B follow-up: the 12-issue taxonomy is a checklist for when a stored subgoal can be wrongly reused.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Soar uses one mechanism for deliberation and meta-reasoning, unlike architectures with separate meta modules (MIDCA, Clarion). Retrieval from episodic and semantic memory and simulation can be done inside a substate.
numbers: qualitative
quote: Soar commits to a single approach for both deliberation and meta-reasoning
limits: Claim is architectural, with no head-to-head test in this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports using the same loop for subgoals as for the main task, as S6 does.

source: Newell (1990) Unified Theories of Cognition; Laird, Newell & Rosenbloom (1987) Soar: an architecture for general intelligence (seen only through citations and summaries)
finding: Universal subgoaling: any difficulty creates a goal automatically; uniform learning hypothesis: goal-based chunking is the general learning mechanism. The 1987 paper and the book were not retrievable (DTIC links returned no PDF).
numbers: none verified
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Do not cite numbers from these works until opened.

source: Allen (1988) Production system chunking in Soar: case studies in automated learning (NASA JSC report)
finding: A small independent application of Soar to the eight-puzzle with several problem-space representations. Learned runs had fewer decision cycles and rule firings, and a learned system did not chunk again on the same task. Concludes learning is an inherent and beneficial aspect of problem solving.
numbers: one run shown: 21 decision cycles, 46 elaboration cycles before learning; later numbers not extracted
limits: Small run, no statistics.
agent_relevance: Independent users reproduced the basic same-problem-no-second-subgoal effect on toy tasks only.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan & Griffiths (2024) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA)
finding: CoALA describes Soar as a template for language agents: an impasse gives a subgoal and hierarchical decomposition; Soar can write new productions into procedural memory. It treats Voyager as an agent that adds code procedures to procedural memory after a success.
numbers: survey; no measured results on impasse or chunking
quote: Soar creates a subgoal to resolve the impasse
limits: Description only; no test of impasse-driven triggers in LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Confirms the mapping: skill library equals procedural memory, and success is the trigger for adding. Impasse as the trigger is not what Voyager does.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec: a cognitive recommender agent fusing large language models and Soar
finding: Closest direct use: when Soar hits a tie impasse it sends the state to an LLM; the answer is parsed into a condition-action chunk and compiled into a new production, so later similar states need no LLM call. Ablations: no LLM bootstrap drops performance sharply; no chunking drops it toward the LLM-only baseline; LLM call frequency falls to a low plateau with chunking but stays high without.
numbers: Dataset example ML-1M: 6,040 users, 3,416 items, 999,611 interactions; exact metric values and ablation numbers not recoverable from the extracted text (figures only)
limits: Offline recommendation, not reasoning. Results read only qualitatively. Built and tested by the same authors; no outside replication.
agent_relevance: Best existing LLM + impasse + chunk demonstration. It shows the call-cost saving, not that the compiled rules are correct. We need a verify step they lack.

source: From cognitive architectures to language agents: a mechanism-level review (arXiv 2607.23942, 2026)
finding: Compares ACT-R and Soar mechanisms with modern agents. Soar's chain is typed impasse, protected substate, typed result return, chunk. The review says modern systems copy only parts: PALADIN and AgentDebugX (typed failure to recovery), Shepherd (protected branch), AgentHER and Reflexion (experience changes later behavior, but detached from a typed impasse).
numbers: review table rows; no new measurements
limits: Only a partial skim of this long review; claims about each system are the reviewer's, not verified against those papers.
agent_relevance: Gap map: no listed system has all four links. A scaffold that does would be new.

source: SoK: agentic skills beyond tool use in LLM agents (arXiv 2602.20867, 2026)
finding: Survey that cites a skills benchmark (SkillsBench): curated skills raise pass rate, self-generated skills do not. This is the main measured warning for any compile-what-you-solved-into-a-reusable-skill design.
numbers: 7 agent-model configurations, 7,308 trajectories; curated skills +16.2 points (24.3% to 40.6%); by domain healthcare +51.9, manufacturing +41.9, cybersecurity +23.2, software engineering +4.5, mathematics +6.0; self-generated skills -1.3 points on average (Opus 4.6 +1.4; Codex with GPT-5.2 -5.6); 2-3 skills +18.6, 4+ skills +5.9; comprehensive skills -2.9
quote: models cannot yet reliably author the procedural knowledge they benefit from consuming
limits: Secondhand numbers via a survey; the benchmark paper was not opened. Self-generated here means the model writes skills before the task, not after an impasse, so it is not an exact test of chunking.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against auto-saving every solved subgoal. Gate entries by a passed test and keep the library small.

source: Lotem & Halpern (2025) Evolution of diverse cognitive abilities through adaptive fine-tuning of learning and chunking mechanisms
finding: Opened only to its title and first lines. A formal model of chunking as a general learning mechanism in evolution, not about Soar impasses.
numbers: none read
limits: Out of scope for this subfield; listed so it is not mistaken for an impasse study.
agent_relevance: None for now.

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1987b) Learning by chunking: a production system model of practice (as cited by Heathcote et al. 2000)
finding: Cited in the 2000 survey: for a single subject on Seibel's task the exponential fit better than both the power and general-power functions. So the chunking authors' own later fit did not support the power law for that subject.
numbers: single subject; details in the 1987b paper not opened
limits: Secondhand through Heathcote et al.; the 1987b paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat power-law predictions of chunk benefit as a hypothesis only.
